title: Macklemore calls for a ‘free Palestine’ during Ed Sheeran shows, prompting praise and backlash
summary:
Macklemore calls for a ‘free Palestine’ during Ed Sheeran shows, prompting praise and backlash

Rights advocates, journalists and social media users have come out in support of the American rapper Macklemore in response to pressure from pro-Israelgroups for expressing support for Palestine in his opening act performances for Ed Sheeran in the United States.

Footage from Gaza and the occupied West Bank was displayed on screens as Macklemore, whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty, performed in front of more than 80,000 people in MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Friday and Saturday as part of English singer-songwriter Sheeran's Loop tour. 

Macklemore performed "Hind’s Hall", a pro-Palestine anthem in support of anti-genocide campus protests in the US, and named after five-year-old Hind Rajab, who was shot and killed by Israeli forces in Gaza in 2024.

title: Palestinian child killed by Israel on first day back at school in Gaza
summary:
Palestinian child killed by Israel on first day back at school in Gaza

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 09/07/2026 - 18:07
Wafaa Akila, aged eight, was photographed smiling in her blue school uniform hours before an Israeli strike killed the little girl and her father
Images of eight-year-old Palestinian girl Wafaa Akila are circulating on social media after an Israeli strike killed her alongside her father in Gaza City on Sunday (Social media/X)
Off

An eight-year-old Palestinian girl, whose age was confirmed by al-Shifa hospital, was killed alongside her father in an Israeli strike on Gaza City on Sunday, hours after she attended the first day of the new school year.

Wafaa Yousef Nabil Akila and her father, Youssef Nabil Rabah Akila, were travelling in a vehicle in western Gaza City when an Israeli drone near the Hamid intersection struck the car.

The attack also wounded six other Palestinians, according to medical officials at al-Shifa hospital.

Photographs shared before the strike showed Wafaa smiling in a blue school uniform and giving a thumbs-up on her first day back at school.

Eight-year-old Wafaa Akila was killed alongside her father on her first day of school when an Israeli strike hit their car in western Gaza.

The IDF insists the attack was targeting a "Hamas militant." pic.twitter.com/sneFKgoSsV

— HatsOff (@HatsOffff) September 7, 2026

Images from the aftermath showed her schoolbooks and supplies scattered across the charred wreckage of the vehicle.

Footage published by Drop Site News showed men at the scene holding strands of the child's hair.

“This is all that’s left, world,” one man said in the footage. “What truce are you talking about?”

“There has been no ceasefire,” another said. “Every day there are massacres. Every day there is killing. Every day children are dying.”

“Enough of this abandonment.”

Many people online reacted with outrage to the attacks, specifically pointing to the fact that the alleged ceasefire has never come into effect in Gaza and civilians continue dying. 

🟥 WAFAA YOUSEF AKILA WAS NINE YEARS OLD. SHE NEVER MADE IT TO HER SECOND DAY OF SCHOOL.

🔳 Yesterday was nine-year-old Wafaa Yousef Akila first day of the new school year in Gaza. After finishing school, she went with her father, Yousef Akila, to buy school supplies for the… pic.twitter.com/kK72ae12GR

— shameen suleman (@shameensuleman) September 7, 2026

The Israeli military initially said the strike had targeted a Hamas member and that it was examining its outcome.

On Monday, it identified Youssef Akila as a company commander in Hamas's elite Nukhba force and accused him of planning attacks against Israeli soldiers and civilians and of working to restore the group's capabilities.

The military did not provide publicly available evidence to substantiate those claims in its announcement.

‘Back to school’ in Gaza

Wafaa's killing prompted anger online, with Palestinians and supporters contrasting the familiar images of children returning to classrooms at the start of an academic year with the continuing killing of children in Gaza.

She asked for nothing more than the chance to learn… yet she was killed. 💔

This is the beautiful little girl, Wafaa Aqilah, whose photo you see before you.

Today, she went out with her father to buy school supplies, carrying the joy of returning to the classroom and the… pic.twitter.com/K1Hk1bmAZs

— Abdullah Omar🇵🇸 (@Abdullah_Om3r03) September 6, 2026

Formal schooling in Gaza is due to resume later in September, though some schools and alternative education centres have already reopened.

Much of Gaza's education infrastructure has been destroyed or damaged by the Israeli military, forcing thousands of Palestinian children to study in tents, makeshift classrooms and buildings also being used as shelters.

For Wafaa, the return to school lasted only hours.

Other children killed across Gaza on Sunday 

Wafaa was one of several Palestinians killed in Israeli attacks across the Gaza Strip on the same day, despite a US-backed ceasefire that came into effect in October 2025.

In central Gaza, seven-year-old Saadi Ghaliya was killed when Israeli artillery struck the Sakina School, which was sheltering displaced families east of Deir al-Balah. Others were wounded in the attack.

In Gaza City, Mohammad Atef Arafat Sukkar, 28, was killed in an Israeli drone strike near a telecommunications junction in the Rimal area, according to Palestinian reports.

Hassan Ali Saqallah, 19, later died from wounds sustained after being shot near Palestine Stadium and al-Mamounia School.

title: Report: US official says Hormuz fully open, under US control
summary:
Report: US official says Hormuz fully open, under US control

The Strait of Hormuz is fully open and under US Navy control, a US official told Al Jazeera.

The official said the assessment follows a covert US Navy mine-clearing operation in the Strait since April, adding that shipping traffic is expected to increase as a result.

The US remains satisfied with current oil and gas flows through the strait, the official said.

title: US presence in Gulf 'not enough' for security, Qatari official says
summary:
US presence in Gulf 'not enough' for security, Qatari official says

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 09/07/2026 - 17:12
Foreign ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari seemed to encourage a diversification away from sole reliance on Washington
Qatar's foreign ministry spokesperson, Majed al-Ansari, attends a session at the Hili Forum 2026 in Abu Dhabi, UAE, on 7 September 2026 (Fadel Senna/AFP)
Off

Qatari foreign ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari on Monday appeared to indicate that the presence of US forces in the Gulf is no longer the protective shield it was once believed to be.

Qatar hosts the largest US military base in the Arab world, which is also the regional headquarters for US Central Command. It has borne the brunt of repeated Iranian retaliatory attacks for the US-Israeli war on the Islamic Republic, which began on 28 February.

"We need to realise in the Gulf that having international forces in the region, having a strategic alliance with the United States, is very important, but is not enough," he said during the Hili Forum in Abu Dhabi, UAE. 

"Self-sufficiency when it comes to security is the only way forward. Yes, we need our partners. Yes, we need our allies. But we cannot depend on them alone for our security," he added.

His comments come as Avril Haines, the former US director of national intelligence under President Joe Biden, told the Financial Times Festival over the weekend that a reduction of the US footprint in the region would spell more trouble than remaining fully engaged.

"Honestly, when you try to pull away from it, and you sort of minimise to the greatest degree your resource allocation, often it doesn’t work out well, is what you see," Haines said. 

Thousands of US military and embassy personnel were evacuated from the Gulf earlier this year as Iran ramped up its retaliation against US assets and energy infrastructure in the region. It's unclear whether they will all return.

Qatar-Iran ties 

In an interview with the Emirati paper, The National, Ansari acknowledged that rebuilding trust with Iran will take time, but it remains necessary because Iran will always be a neighbour.

"As we have found peace and harmony with all of the nationalities living in our countries, we will for sure find a way of living next to Iran," he said. 

Vance: US investigating strike on Iran wedding 'very fully'
Read More »

"Most of the responsibility for that lies on the Iranian side – in exercising good neighbourly relations and realising that they are living next to neighbours, not enemies, and that using military pressure or any other means of pressure will not deliver the results they seek for the people they should be working for," he added. 

"Our goal is to extend our hands when the time is right, and at the same time to keep the deterrence and show very clearly, as we have shown during this crisis, that we are able to defend ourselves."

Despite reassurances for months from US President Donald Trump that the conflict - which his administration does not want to label a "war" - will be over "soon", Ansari warned that its days must be numbered.

"The world cannot afford for this conflict to continue. The world cannot afford for the Strait of Hormuz to remain closed. Our region cannot afford for missiles to go back and forth across the Gulf," he said.

Last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent alluded to the strait as becoming "worthless" in two years' time, when oil pipelines are constructed to bypass it. 

But Ansari insisted the waterway will remain a vital passage regardless of the alternatives being devised around it. 

"The Strait of Hormuz has been a crossroad for international trade for millennia. No one action or situation will change that," Ansari told The National.

He also disagreed with Washington's "Operation Economic Outcast" strategy of ratcheting up sanctions on Iran to "asphyxiate" it, as Bessent had described.

"We have seen economic sanctions in Iraq, Libya and other countries,” Ansari said. "It has never delivered a straightforward desired outcome. For us, a straightforward desired outcome will happen" at the negotiation table, he added.

title: Two Alleged ‘TeamPCP’ Hackers Arrested in Australia
summary:
Authorities in Australia have arrested two men believed to be members of TeamPCP, a prolific cybercrime and data extortion group blamed for perpetrating the longest running spree of software supply chain attacks ever.

In a statement released today, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) said two unnamed suspects from Western Australia, aged 21 and 23, were arrested in connection with a "sophisticated cybercrime syndicate that allegedly created malicious open-source software to rob thousands of global businesses."

The AFP did not name the defendants, but KrebsOnSecurity learned the 21-year-old suspect's real identity in June, and has been communicating with him ever since. This story includes interviews with TeamPCP's self-described spokesperson, and examines clues left behind by the TeamPCP leader that likely led to his undoing.

title: Using a VM to Contain an AI Agent

It won’t work:

My suspicion was that GPT 5.6-Cyber would succeed, but the frequency and manner of its success removed all doubt. We have to reassess sandboxing quality for capable AI agents, and in general the software stack with which they interact.

An off-the-shelf VM is not enough to contain a modern, cyber-capable AI agent. There is simply too much attack surface. Even innocuous features (like running with a display) add extra, exploitable attack surface.

title: Security Vulnerability in a Voting System
summary:
It’s a vulnerability that allows someone to recover the order of ballots cast, newly exploited with AI tools.

Nearly four years since the original vulnerability was disclosed, I was still able to use it to analyze voter behavior in Georgia (one of the 21 states that uses affected scanners) in the recent May 2026 primary.

Notably, I never touched a voting machine, exploited a network, examined source code, or accessed anything non-public.

After pointing a coding agent to the original vulnerability paper, I supplied it with two data sources highlighted in the paper: the early-voting list for each county, and the “CVR” (cast-vote record) file, containing every ballot and its selections (but not the voters’ names or other identifying information). The CVR file is available upon request, precisely because a public, ballot-level record is what makes election results independently verifiable...

title: US immigration policy is coming for your Saturday night plans
summary:
US immigration policy is coming for your Saturday night plans

Submitted by Sumayya Tobah on Mon, 09/07/2026 - 16:26
Visa problems postponing Saint Levant and Wegz's concert tours predate Trump, and Arab Americans cannot treat the crackdown as someone else's issue
Palestinian-Algerian artist Saint Levant performs at the 59th Carthage International Festival at the Roman Theatre of Carthage, near Tunis, on 5 August 2025 (Fethi Belaid/AFP)
Off

It's an early Tuesday morning, and everyone has something to say in my group chats.

Palestinian-Algerian artist Saint Levant has just announced the postponement of the North American leg of his highly anticipated Afandi tour, his first United States tour since 2024, citing visa issues.

"For the last couple of years, I've been having major US visa issues," the artist wrote in an Instagram caption. "After the initial approval of my visa application to come see you in the US, I've been unexpectedly asked to undergo additional background checks, which could take a number of months."

Less than six hours later, Egyptian rapper Wegz made a similar announcement: his US tour dates were postponed until further notice because "visa processing took longer than expected".

The outcry on social media - and in my personal group chats - was instantaneous.

This is not the first (or the last) time that US immigration policy has disrupted the careers of Middle Eastern artists. Last August, Moroccan-Belgian singer Dystinct postponed his North American tour due to visa delays, and a month later, Yusuf Islam, better known as Cat Stevens, delayed his own, citing visa issues.

In November 2024, Palestinian singer Zeyne was detained on her way to perform at US rapper Macklemore's high-profile Gaza fundraiser.

All those incidents were just as alarming, yet most received comparatively little coverage or attention.

Zeyne's detention, it should be noted, happened under the Biden administration.

That distinction matters. While the Trump administration has dramatically escalated immigration enforcement and restrictions, the problems facing immigrants, travellers and Middle Eastern communities did not begin in January 2025.

A conflicted community

Arab Americans have a conflicted, well-documented relationship with US immigration policies.

Perhaps more surprising, particularly for a population made up largely of immigrants and their descendants, is how many Arab Americans hold conservative views on immigration.

According to an Arab News-YouGov survey, 56 percent of respondents said US border controls should be tightened, and 51 percent said there are too many undocumented immigrants in the country - views held in even higher proportions by Arab Americans over 55.

'This issue doesn't impact us' was a sentiment I heard repeated early and often - and it could not be more misinformed

This repetition of Republican talking points is alarming, showing just how removed our communities consider themselves from such narratives and the policies they shape.

And while most Arabs in the US were born here, about 68 percent of foreign-born Arabs are US citizens, according to the Brookings Institution.

Our communities are facing a reckoning on immigration, and the politics are far from straightforward. According to the same Brookings analysis, the economy and the war on Gaza were the top issues among Arab Americans during the 2024 election, with Gaza ranking first among Arab-American Democrats.

I came face to face with these perspectives during my time as a journalist on the road covering the 2024 election. Our communities, filled with so many contradictions around identity and belonging, often viewed immigration and its enforcement as issues somewhere on the periphery.

"This issue doesn't impact us" was a sentiment I heard repeated early and often - and it could not be more misinformed.

No one is exempt

Among Arab Americans, the misconception persists that only the undocumented have something to lose under this administration's policies.

But Jesse Franzblau, associate policy director at the National Immigrant Justice Center, told me that the administration's immigration policies are affecting people who are legally present in the US, as well as those who are considering coming here.

"There's so many people, you know, students who are just deciding not to come, also, and then students who are here are deciding to leave because of the risk," Franzblau said.

That risk extends to artists, too.

View on Instagram

"When you see these high-profile cases of musicians that don't come because they're not able to get visas, or often they're not able to get visas for all of the people in their crew. It's just not worth it to come to the US for the risk," Franzblau added.

Under the second Trump administration, the crackdown has been severe.

US President Donald Trump has expanded his original travel ban to impose full or partial restrictions on nationals of 39 countries, many of them in Africa and the Middle East, as well as people travelling on Palestinian Authority-issued documents.

Domestically, raids by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have terrorised immigrant and Latino communities.

The climate is now so hostile that Bad Bunny, the Grammy-winning global superstar who headlined the 2026 Super Bowl halftime show, excluded the continental US from his world tour amid concerns about immigration raids and the safety of his fans.

Closer to home

This administration has no intention of curbing the expansion of ICE detentions. In February, it announced plans for a 500-bed detention facility in Romulus, Michigan - a mere 25-minute drive from Dearborn, home to the largest concentration of Arab Americans in the United States.

The plan was abandoned in June, but only after the state of Michigan and the city of Romulus sued - and the warehouse was one of 11 ICE had bought across the country for detention, with at least four still moving ahead.

Let's not forget Mahmoud Khalil, detained for months over his Palestinian advocacy, or Leqaa Kordia, who spent a year in ICE custody before her release in March.

How US counterterror doctrine turned Minneapolis into a war zone
Read More »

Since returning to office, Trump has moved quickly to overhaul the US immigration system: expanding expedited deportations nationwide; deploying 1,500 more active-duty troops to the southern border; restricting access to asylum; halting refugee resettlement; and reinstating the "Remain in Mexico" policy.

He also scrapped CBP One, the Customs and Border Protection app that migrants used to schedule appointments with border agents, stranding some 30,000 people in Mexico whose appointments were already booked.

His administration has expanded ICE's enforcement powers, too, reversing a longstanding guideline that prohibited immigration raids in areas deemed "sensitive", such as schools, hospitals and churches.

Together, the changes amount to a sweeping effort to make it harder to enter the country, harder to seek protection and easier for the government to detain and deport people already here.

Even if it did not affect us - even if it affected only our friends, our neighbours or the strangers we pass on the street - this administration is stripping dignity from people simply trying to build better lives for themselves and their families.

As Franzblau put it: "There is very much [a] divide-and-conquer type of strategy by this administration in their approach, tearing at the social fabric of communities, which has a deeply divisive impact."

With the latest headlines about the postponement of both Saint Levant's and Wegz's upcoming tours, I pray this moment serves as a motivator for my community come November's midterm elections.

I'm glad we're paying attention. Now I hope that attention carries into the voting booth.

title: Israeli clearance of Gaza rubble could destroy 'evidence', says UN expert
summary:
Israeli clearance of Gaza rubble could destroy 'evidence', says UN expert

A United Nations expert said on Monday that Israeli clearance of rubble in Gaza could destroy valuable evidence of "atrocity crimes" and prevent the recovery of human remains.

Francesca Albanese, the UN expert on the Palestinian territories, said evidence should be gathered and human remains identified before full clearance started.

She issued a statement headlined: "UN expert warns Israeli rubble-clearing could erase traces of atrocity crimes", and said Palestinians should be behind any plans to remove waste.

"In devastated Gaza, rubble is not just construction waste. It is part of a crime scene, a graveyard, and the material record of what happened during a brutal and senseless bombing campaign that lasted two years,” she said.

She said that multiple sources had confirmed Israeli companies were involved in the clearance, without naming those sources.

title: Germany asks ICJ to dismiss Gaza genocide case brought by Nicaragua
summary:
Germany asks ICJ to dismiss Gaza genocide case brought by Nicaragua

Germany asked the International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Monday to dismiss a case accusing it of facilitating genocide in Gaza through its military support for Israel.

Berlin told the UN's supreme judicial body that Nicaragua had failed to establish the existence of a legal dispute before bringing proceedings in March 2024 and that parts of the case fell outside the court’s jurisdiction.

"Nicaragua’s conduct indicates that it was not interested in hearing Germany’s view on its allegations, but simply in bringing Germany before this court," Julia Monar, legal adviser at the German foreign ministry, told judges.

title: UN rights chief urges end to arms sales to Israel
summary:
UN rights chief urges end to arms sales to Israel

UN human rights chief Volker Turk has urged states to end weapons sales to Israel.

“They need to end the transfer to Israel of arms that risk being used to violate international law. Companies also need to end business practices that support illegal settlements,” he said.
